title: Conversation portability layer: request shaping + function-call reconciliation
creator: Ava Chen
description: Create a portability layer that accepts OpenAI Chat Completions style requests and reliably maps them to Redwood's internal streaming + function-calling surface. Goals: preserve streaming semantics, guarantee function-call determinism, map structured outputs into Redwood canonical schema, and minimize surprises for legacy clients while enabling newer Redwood features (KV caching hints, explicit rollout tokens).
acceptance_criteria: 1) Redwood API accepts legacy Chat Completions request bodies and returns semantically equivalent completions for non-toolcall flows (text + streaming).

2) Tool/function calling: calls encoded in OA-style requests must map to Redwood tool invocation API and produce identical ordered events in the streamed response, including function call start/end markers and intermediate deltas.
3) Structured outputs produced by models via OA-style 'response_format' hints must be transformed to Redwood's structured-output envelope with schema validation and failure fallback.
4) Backwards compatibility: existing client integrations using OpenAI SDKs that hit the portability layer should not require SDK changes for common flows (chat, streaming, simple tool calls).
5) Telemetry: every mapped request must emit a mapping_version tag and per-request delta showing fields dropped, renamed, or defaulted.
6) Security: input sanitization and function whitelist enforcement must pass security review before rollout.
technical_summary: We will implement a stateless request shaper sitting in the request ingestion pipeline that performs: 1) request normalization (role field harmonization, stop token translation, temperature defaults), 2) streaming frame mapping (convert OA framed tokens/deltas into Redwood streaming events while preserving chunk boundaries), 3) function-call reconciliation (map OA 'function_call' directives to Redwood tool descriptors, enforce allowlist, and surface tool metadata into the stream), and 4) structured-output wrapper (validate JSON/YAML outputs against Redwood schemas and wrap with metadata). The shaper will emit fine-grained telemetry and a mapping_version header to enable progressive rollouts and quick rollbacks.
rollout_plan: Phase A (internal): route 5% of OA-compat traffic from staging to the new portability layer for smoke tests (monitor differences vs canonical pipeline). Phase B (beta): opt-in customer list + feature flag for 25% production traffic. Phase C: global opt-out fallback disabled, audit for 2 weeks, then full migration. Backout: route flag to bypass shaper and run through canonical translator if diffs exceed threshold.
test_plan: Unit tests for request normalization rules (role coercion, system message handling, prompt truncation).
Integration tests comparing outputs between canonical Redwood pipeline and OA-compat pipeline across a representative prompt corpus (test vectors in repo/tests/compat).
Stream fuzz tests: randomized chunking and partial token sequences to ensure streaming frame deterministic mapping.
Tool call E2E: simulated tool endpoints verifying call/response ordering, idempotency markers, and error propagation semantics.
Schema validation tests for structured outputs with graceful fallback to text mode when parsing fails.
notes: Trade-offs considered: 1) Deeply emulating OA behavior increases surface area for subtle differences (we aim for behavioral parity only for common flows and provide explicit opt-ins for legacy edge behaviors). 2) We selected a stateless shaper to avoid adding persistent transformation state; persistent state would simplify some idempotency guarantees but raise rollout complexity. 3) For streaming, we preserve OA-style partial content ordering but annotate every event with a redwood_event_id for observability.
